rewrites.blindSummary:
This country is dangerous for trans visitors. It is the site of the region's defining transfemicide case: a trans woman and activist shot dead in 2009, whose case reached the regional human-rights court — which in 2021 found the national authorities themselves responsible for her death and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime. The ruling ordered reforms (including legal gender recognition, which the country has partially implemented), but violence against LGBT people remains at levels a human-rights organisation called “epidemic,” driving mass asylum-seeking.

Nothing criminalises being trans, and the ruling created formal obligations; a name-change process exists. But gangs, security forces, and social actors all contribute to a documented pattern of violence against trans women in particular, and prosecution remains rare.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, but outing-violence probability is among the highest in the region, outside the two largest countries.

The consequence axis of an arrest is one of the region's most dangerous documented elements: the country places transgender women in the men's prison system — birth-sex placement with no placement-by-gender-identity policy, documented in 2017 and independently confirmed in 2020. At the national penitentiary, LGBTI prisoners were concentrated in one module beside the mentally-ill unit, where trans women were forced to cut their hair, barred from presenting as women, and denied conjugal visits; at another facility, authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after the national torture-prevention centre intervened was she isolated from the men and her belongings returned. An international human-rights organisation states the practice “can lead to physical and sexual abuse,” and documents a local judge's account of a trans woman raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards — prosecutors were informed and did not investigate (“There's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons”). A detained trans visitor therefore faces male-facility placement with documented sexual-violence risk and official inaction, matching the record's already severe street-level warning.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Regional comparison: a rights-law report groups this nation with a neighbouring nation among the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, and regional nations have long excluded trans women from femicide-justice frameworks — the pattern that made this case the leading one of its kind.

Justice-system context: documented impunity is driven by under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and intentional case mishandling — the enforcement backdrop for anyone assessing risk.

Custody-axis documentation trail: the placement practice is documented twice, five years apart — 2017 reporting by a trans activist drawing on the national torture-prevention centre, and an international human-rights organisation's 2020 three-country report independently confirming that trans women are placed in men's prisons where abuse can follow; the judge-reported rape with guards' complicity and no prosecution is the enforcement context inside the system, not a visitor-facing protection.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The court-ordered legal-gender-recognition reform (partially implemented) and the name-change process are resident-facing; the epidemic-level violence and mass asylum-seeking describe residents' situation.

Resident-facing documentation: trans people have faced police assault, extortion and worse for years, and politically visible trans people have faced threats and attacks, with at least one organiser seeking asylum abroad.

The custody practice is resident-facing: trans women held in the national penitentiaries' men's system — a concentration module with its forced hair-cutting and dress suppression, a separate seizure of clothing and hair, and the judge-reported rape with guards' complicity and no investigation — all fall on residents in national custody; a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope:
Unresolved: how the documented gang and security-force violence applies to short-stay visitors in tourist contexts is not quantified in the current sources — gang violence affects everyone.
Unverified: no documented trans-visitor incidents appear in the current sources; the responsibility finding covers an individual case and signals institutional accountability rather than a visitor-specific enforcement pattern.
Prison axis: no national statute, regulation or department policy fixing trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented — the placement practice rests on the 2017 and 2020 documentation; the concentration module is a de facto arrangement rather than a codified special unit; and whether the documented practices persist as of the research date is unverified.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This country demands real caution from trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years, among the lowest anywhere; the case of a trans woman deported from abroad and killed became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, the president's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is an exceptional security regime with mass arbitrary detention (tens of thousands imprisoned, over 75,000 reported, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented and grim: since the exceptional security regime began (March 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in the mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. The only documented custody case (2024 investigative reporting): a trans woman arrested in April 2022 was held at police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out with another trans woman for outdoor punishment drills (handcuffed, forced squatting in the sun), and denied her HIV clinic access; a judge freed her after about four months, finding the arrest unsupported, while the second trans woman remained imprisoned. The exceptional-security-regime risk mechanism is therefore not hypothetical in custody: it is where the regime's arbitrary power meets identity-based mistreatment, with no special custody provision documented and release dependent on judicial review.
rewrites.blindTangential:
Regional comparison: a 2020 human-rights report groups this nation with two neighbouring nations as failing to effectively address violence and entrenched discrimination against LGBT people, driving asylum claims abroad.

Legislative and research context: 2015 legal-code reforms made bias-motivated killings punishable by long prison sentences; a 2024 longitudinal study profiles homicides against LGBTI+ people across two decades; and the first conviction came in 2020 — legal milestones that do not by themselves change the practical visitor risk.

Custody-axis context: the human-rights organisations documenting the 2022 case link the abuse to the absence of a gender identity law — an explanatory framing, not a policy change — and the case's single recourse point (a judge releasing the detainee for an unsupported arrest while her co-detainee stayed imprisoned) is partial judicial pushback within an otherwise exceptional regime, not a protection a visitor can rely on.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly:
The administrative name-change-only process and the absent legal-gender-recognition law are resident-facing; the historical life-expectancy figure and the killing case described in the summary are resident-facing too.

The documented custody case is resident-facing: the two trans women held after the April 2022 raid (one released by a judge after about four months, the other still imprisoned per the 2024 report) were residents in national custody, and the forced head-shaving, punishment drills and denied HIV clinic access fall on residents; a visitor meets the practice only through arrest and detention.

Prison axis: the custody documentation is a single 2024 investigation of one case — no national statute, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) appears in this record, no special custody provision is documented for prisoners captured in the raids, and how widespread the documented mistreatment is across the mass-detention population is unverified.
